title: Sim-to-Real Transfer on the Unitree G1: Domain Randomization & Dynamic Push Recovery
summary: How we train bipedal locomotion policies with randomized friction, motor delays, and ground inclination in simulation to achieve robust zero-shot push recovery on the physical Unitree G1 platform.
contentMarkdown:
# Sim-to-Real Transfer on the Unitree G1: Domain Randomization & Dynamic Push Recovery

Deploying reinforcement learning (RL) policies directly onto a physical humanoid biped platform like the **Unitree G1** is notoriously prone to the reality gap. In simulation, contact physics are idealized, actuator dynamics are instantaneous, and sensor readings have minimal covariance noise. On real hardware, motor thermal states shift internal winding resistance, bus latencies fluctuate over CAN/Ethernet, and physical foot-ground impacts produce high-frequency vibrations that degrade IMU state estimates.

Here is how we closed that gap at FEV India to achieve reliable zero-shot dynamic walking and balance stabilization on physical hardware.

---

## 1. Domain Randomization Strategy

Rather than attempting to model physical hardware down to the sub-millimeter, we envelope real-world parameter variance during parallelized training in physics simulators (such as NVIDIA Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab):

- **Ground Friction Coefficient**: Uniformly sampled across $[0.3, 1.25]$ to simulate slick epoxy factory flooring, carpet, and rough concrete.
- **Payload & Center of Mass (CoM)**: Base mass randomized by $\pm 2.5\text{ kg}$ and CoM position displaced by up to $\pm 35\text{ mm}$ along the longitudinal and lateral axes.
- **Actuator Latency**: Injected variable transport delays between $10\text{ ms}$ and $35\text{ ms}$ into the policy action execution queue to mirror physical bus queuing.
- **Joint Damping & Stiffness**: Joint stiffness ($K_p$) and damping ($K_d$) randomized by $\pm 15\%$ around nominal gains to prevent policies from overfitting to razor-sharp PD controller responses.

```python
# Domain Randomization configuration excerpt
randomization_params = {
    'static_friction': ('uniform', 0.35, 1.2),
    'base_mass_offset': ('uniform', -2.0, 2.5),  # kg
    'action_delay_steps': ('randint', 1, 4),       # 20ms steps
    'joint_friction': ('uniform', 0.85, 1.15),
    'push_velocity_magnitude': ('uniform', 0.2, 0.8) # m/s impulse
}
```

---

## 2. Multi-Tiered Safety Architecture

A runaway policy on a quadruped might result in a rolled chassis; on a 35kg bipedal humanoid, an uncontrolled joint snap can destroy planetary reduction gears or crack knee links. We enforce a hardware-level safety interceptor between the neural policy and joint drivers:

1. **Kinematic Workspace Boundaries**: Software limit envelopes preventing joint self-collisions between thighs, calves, and the Inspire dexterous hand.
2. **Dynamic Torque Clamps**: Instantaneous motor current monitoring that shuts down joint power if torque demand exceeds $85\%$ of peak rated capacity for more than $20\text{ ms}$.
3. **IMU Divergence Watchdog**: If pitch or roll exceeds $28^\circ$ from vertical, the controller automatically triggers a compliant squat-and-catch safe fall reflex.

---

## 3. Results on Physical Hardware

Across over 40 physical push-recovery trials:
- **Lateral Impulse Rejection**: The G1 successfully recovered balance from lateral pushes up to $0.6\text{ m/s}$ without triggering emergency falls.
- **Terrain Transition**: Clean transition from polished vinyl flooring onto $15\text{ mm}$ textured obstacles without re-tuning gain matrices.

The key takeaway: **A policy that anticipates physical imperfection in simulation is the only policy that survives on real hardware.**

title: Slashing Perception Latency by 80%: Migrating Python Hot Paths to Multithreaded C++ on Jetson AGX
summary: Profiling the 195ms latency crisis in a multi-camera industrial perception stack, uncovering memory copy bottlenecks, and restructuring into a 42ms zero-copy C++ pipeline running on edge Jetson hardware.
contentMarkdown:
# Slashing Perception Latency by 80%: Migrating Python Hot Paths to Multithreaded C++ on Jetson AGX

At Wastefull Insights, our autonomous waste sorting facility relied on 4 concurrent 1080p RTSP camera streams monitoring high-speed conveyor belts. The robots had less than $350\text{ ms}$ between when an item was first imaged by the overhead cameras and when the picking arm had to initiate its descent trajectory.

Our initial Python-based perception pipeline was struggling: total frame-to-decision latency was **195ms**, and GPU utilization was pinned at **95%** on expensive desktop-class RTX graphics cards. In this article, I break down how profiling the system revealed the real bottleneck, and how we cut latency to **42ms** on low-power Jetson AGX hardware.

---

## 1. The Profiling Breakdown: The Latency Crisis

Before changing a single line of code, we profiled the pipeline using NVIDIA Nsight Systems and PyTorch CUDA profilers. The results were illuminating:

| Pipeline Stage | Implementation | Time Taken | % of Budget |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| RTSP Ingestion & Decode | Python OpenCV VideoCapture | 5 ms | 2.5% |
| GPU Pre-Processing & Scaling | NumPy / Python CPU copies | 50 ms | 25.6% |
| Neural Model Inference | PyTorch FP32 YOLOv5 | 80 ms | 41.0% |
| Bounding Box Tracking & NMS | Python loops / Shapely | 60 ms | 30.8% |
| **Total Frame-to-Pick Latency** | | **195 ms** | **100%** |

Notice that **110ms out of 195ms** had nothing to do with neural model computation! It was completely consumed by Python interpreter overhead, host-to-device memory copies (`cudaMemcpy`), and inefficient CPU polygon operations.

---

## 2. Four Steps to 42ms Latency

### Step 1: Model Quantization with TensorRT (80ms → 35ms)
We exported the trained YOLOv5 weights into ONNX and compiled an optimized TensorRT engine with **FP16 precision** and calibrated **INT8 layers** for backbone convolutions:
- Layer fusion eliminated unnecessary memory round-trips to VRAM.
- Kernel auto-tuning selected optimal CUDA kernel configurations for the Jetson AGX Xavier GPU architecture.

### Step 2: Zero-Copy Hardware Decoding via DeepStream (50ms → 2ms)
We eliminated Python's CPU decode buffer. Using NVIDIA DeepStream SDK, video streams from all 4 cameras were decoded directly into NVMM (NVIDIA Memory Management) hardware memory. Frames stayed in GPU memory from initial H.264 decode through TensorRT inference—**zero CPU-GPU transfers**.

### Step 3: Multithreaded C++ Hot Paths (60ms → 5ms)
We rewrote the post-processing tracking, non-maximum suppression (NMS), conveyor line-crossing triggers, and multi-robot task allocation in modern **C++20**:
- Lock-free ring buffers (`std::atomic`) for frame metadata.
- SIMD-accelerated polygon intersection checks for overlapping recyclable materials.

### Step 4: Asynchronous Double-Buffering
Implemented asynchronous CUDA streams (`cudaStream_t`) so camera capture of frame $N+1$ overlapped seamlessly with TensorRT inference on frame $N$.

---

## 3. Quantified Impact

```
Before Optimization (Desktop RTX):
Latency: 195ms | GPU Load: 95% | Hardware Cost: $$$$

After Optimization (Jetson AGX Xavier):
Latency: 42ms  | GPU Load: 20% | Hardware Cost: $ (4x reduction)
```

**The takeaway:** In robotics, algorithm architecture and memory layout will always matter more than raw compute horsepower.

title: 240 FPS Trajectory Prediction: Real-Time Computer Vision for Robotic Air Hockey
summary: Designing a 240 FPS puck-tracking pipeline that executes trajectory forecasting, rebound angle calculation, and striker intercept kinematics within 7ms to beat human opponents.
contentMarkdown:
# 240 FPS Trajectory Prediction: Real-Time Computer Vision for Robotic Air Hockey

During my time commissioning exhibits for India's first public Robotics Gallery at Gujarat Science City, one of the most demanding real-time platforms was the **4-DOF SCARA Air Hockey Robot**. Unlike industrial robots picking stationary parts, an air hockey puck travels at speeds up to $8\text{ m/s}$ ($28.8\text{ km/h}$) with unpredictable acoustic rebounds off aluminum side rails.

To consistently block human shots and return aggressive bank shots, the vision-to-motion control loop had to operate under an ultra-strict deadline: **less than 10 milliseconds from camera photon to motor torque**.

---

## 1. High-Speed Optical Pipeline at 240 FPS

A standard 30 FPS camera captures a frame every $33.3\text{ ms}$. At $8\text{ m/s}$, a puck moves over $26\text{ cm}$ between consecutive frames—rendering trajectory estimation completely useless due to severe motion blur.

We deployed a high-speed global-shutter CMOS camera configured at **240 FPS** ($4.16\text{ ms}$ inter-frame interval) with a localized Region of Interest (ROI):
- **Color Thresholding & HSV Segmentation**: HSV color thresholding was accelerated using lookup tables (LUTs) in memory.
- **Contour Filtering & Centroid Extraction**: Evaluated puck circularity and area to filter out reflections from fluorescent gallery ceiling lights.

---

## 2. Rebound Physics & Intercept Calculation

```
   Puck Vector [X, Y, Vx, Vy] 
            ↓ 
   Wall Collision Detector (Boundary Checks)
            ↓
   Specular Reflection Model (Coefficient of Restitution e = 0.92)
            ↓
   Striker Intercept Kinematics (7ms deadline)
```

When a shot is fired towards the robot goal:
1. We fit a linear least-squares regression line through the last 4 centroid positions to calculate instantaneous velocity components $(V_x, V_y)$.
2. If the vector intersects the side rails, we calculate specular rebound angles modified by an empirical coefficient of restitution ($e = 0.92$).
3. The intercept solver computes where the puck will cross the defensive striking arc, maps Cartesian coordinates to SCARA joint angles $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ via inverse kinematics, and streams velocity commands to the servo drives via ROS.

---

## 3. Production Lessons

Operating this system 8 hours a day with hundreds of museum visitors revealed key lessons:
- **Lighting Stability**: Variations in ambient museum lighting disrupted HSV color masks. We enclosed the table with synchronized high-CRI LED strips and calibrated ambient light offsets daily.
- **Mechanical Settling**: High-speed SCARA arm reversals produced table resonance. Adding S-curve jerk-limiting filters stopped striker ringing and kept defensive block accuracy above $92\%$.

title: Industrial Edge AI: Mitigating Thermal Throttling & Ambient Lighting Shifts on 24/7 Factory Floors
summary: Practical engineering lessons from 24/7 conveyor sorting facilities: positive-pressure cooling enclosures, predictive GPU throttling before thermal trips, and synchronized strobe illumination.
contentMarkdown:
# Industrial Edge AI: Mitigating Thermal Throttling & Ambient Lighting Shifts on 24/7 Factory Floors

Building an AI model that runs on an engineer's air-conditioned development machine is straightforward. Deploying that same model inside an industrial facility where summer ambient temperatures hit $44^\circ\text{C}$, airborne particulate settles on optical lenses, and overhead skylights shift daylight angles continuously is where most robotics projects fail.

Here are the critical reliability patterns we engineered at Wastefull Insights to maintain **99.9% uptime** on factory sorting lines.

---

## 1. The Thermal Throttling Problem

Embedded AI edge processors like the NVIDIA Jetson series are engineered to protect silicon by automatically stepping down core frequencies when junction temperatures exceed $85^\circ\text{C}$:
- As thermal limits are hit, GPU clock rates scale down by up to $50\%$.
- Frame processing time jumps from $42\text{ ms}$ to over $110\text{ ms}$.
- Frames back up in queue buffers, latency accumulates, and the robotic arms miss picking conveyor targets.

### The Engineering Fix:
1. **Positive-Pressure Filtered Enclosure**: We mounted the Jetson modules inside an IP54 sealed enclosure equipped with dual high-static-pressure fans and cleanable HEPA dust filters. Positive pressure prevented conveyor dust from entering the housing.
2. **Dynamic Workload Regulation**: We implemented telemetry monitoring that read GPU thermal zones every $500\text{ ms}$. If temperatures passed $78^\circ\text{C}$, the software dynamically dropped batch size from 4 to 2 and alerted facility technicians before thermal throttling kicked in.
3. **Heat Sink Thermal Interface**: Replaced standard silicone thermal pads with high-conductivity phase-change materials, dropping thermal resistance by $35\%$.

---

## 2. Eliminating Ambient Lighting Noise

One of the most common causes of false positive detections on factory lines is moving shadows cast by workers, forklift headlights, and changing sunlight angles through warehouse skylights.

To eliminate optical variance:
- **Synchronized Strobe Illumination**: We enclosed the primary imaging zone with custom high-lumen LED arrays triggered by hardware optocoupler signals from the camera's GPIO strobe pin.
- **Microsecond Exposure Times**: By strobing light at $80,000\text{ lux}$ for only $150\ \mu\text{s}$, the camera aperture could be narrowed, completely overpowering ambient lighting while freezing high-speed conveyor motion with zero blur.

---

## 3. Summary Rule

In industrial robotics, software cannot compensate for poor hardware design. True system reliability requires co-designing thermal dissipation, optical lighting, and software algorithms into a unified, fault-tolerant whole.
